evidenceAudit.scope: Woman with a perineal tear after vaginal birth: systematic perineal and rectal examination, grading from first to fourth degree, repair of first and second degree tears with local anaesthetic, theatre repair of third and fourth degree tears (obstetric anal sphincter injury, OASIS), antibiotics, laxatives and analgesia, follow-up and advice for a future birth. Uses the Oman Ministry of Health Royal Hospital guideline (based on RCOG Green-top 29) and the Royal Hospital for Women (NSW) business rule; a Saudi single-centre study supplies local incidence. No Saudi national guideline was found.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-14.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health or Saudi Society of Obstetrics and Gynecology guideline on perineal tears was found; the Oman Ministry of Health guideline (a Gulf neighbour that follows RCOG Green-top 29) and the NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule are the clinical sources, and the Jeddah study supplies Saudi incidence only.
The RCOG Green-top Guideline 29 text itself could not be downloaded; its content is taken from the two guidelines above that quote it.

Antibiotic doses and the oral course (cefazolin 2 g, clindamycin 600 mg, metronidazole 500 mg intravenous, co-amoxiclav 875 mg/125 mg twice daily for 5 days) come from the NSW rule; the Oman guideline asks for a 7-day oral course and does not name doses, so the course length differs between sources.
The cefazolin label gives 1 g for pre-operative prophylaxis; the 2 g dose (3 g above 120 kg) is from the NSW rule and exceeds the label dose, so the prescriber should confirm it locally.
The metronidazole injection label gives treatment and colorectal-surgery prophylaxis doses by weight, not a single 500 mg dose; the 500 mg single dose is from the NSW rule.

Lactulose 15 mL twice daily for 10 days to 2 weeks is from the Oman guideline; the US lactulose label covers portal-systemic encephalopathy only, so the obstetric use is off-label and the label supplies contraindications and cautions only.

Lidocaine volume for perineal infiltration and the maximum dose table could not be read from the extracted label text; the volume is titrated to effect within the label maximum, and no millilitre figure is written.

Analgesia (paracetamol, diclofenac, opioid) and ice pack advice are described in the NSW rule but no analgesic regimen is written because of label dose limits that differ from the rule; use the unit formulary.
Suture material and technique (3-0 polyglactin or polydioxanone, overlap or end-to-end) follow the guidelines; no suture product label was reviewed.
Antibiotic alternatives for severe penicillin hypersensitivity after clindamycin (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus metronidazole) are listed in the NSW rule but their labels were not reviewed.
Figures were read by automated extraction of PDF and label text; spot-check each dose against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: During vaginal birth the perineum stretches and tears; the depth decides the grade: skin and mucosa (first), perineal muscle (second), anal sphincter (third), sphincter plus anal lining (fourth) (Oman MOH guideline, Section 02 Classification). The anal sphincter has two layers: the external anal sphincter (EAS) holds back stool voluntarily and the internal anal sphincter (IAS) gives resting tone; torn ends retract and need to be found and sewn together (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5). Unrecognised or poorly repaired sphincter tears are the main cause of later anal incontinence; every skin tear reaching the anal margin is a third degree tear until proven otherwise (Oman MOH guideline, Section 4.0). A tear of the rectal lining alone with an intact sphincter is a rectal buttonhole tear; if missed it can form a rectovaginal fistula (Oman MOH guideline, Section 2.1). Risk is higher with a first vaginal birth, forceps, a baby over 4 kg, persistent occipito-posterior position, shoulder dystocia, midline episiotomy, prolonged second stage and induction (Oman MOH guideline, Section 3.1). Wound infection, haematoma and dehiscence follow poorly supported repairs, constipation and straining, which is why antibiotics, laxatives and good pain relief are given after sphincter repair (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1).
keyMechanisms: During vaginal birth the perineum stretches and tears; the depth decides the grade: skin and mucosa (first), perineal muscle (second), anal sphincter (third), sphincter plus anal lining (fourth) (Oman MOH guideline, Section 02 Classification).

The anal sphincter has two layers: the external anal sphincter (EAS) holds back stool voluntarily and the internal anal sphincter (IAS) gives resting tone; torn ends retract and need to be found and sewn together (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5).

Unrecognised or poorly repaired sphincter tears are the main cause of later anal incontinence; every skin tear reaching the anal margin is a third degree tear until proven otherwise (Oman MOH guideline, Section 4.0).
A tear of the rectal lining alone with an intact sphincter is a rectal buttonhole tear; if missed it can form a rectovaginal fistula (Oman MOH guideline, Section 2.1).

Risk is higher with a first vaginal birth, forceps, a baby over 4 kg, persistent occipito-posterior position, shoulder dystocia, midline episiotomy, prolonged second stage and induction (Oman MOH guideline, Section 3.1).

Wound infection, haematoma and dehiscence follow poorly supported repairs, constipation and straining, which is why antibiotics, laxatives and good pain relief are given after sphincter repair (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1).

symptoms: Perineal pain, burning or a feeling of bulging after birth (clinical judgment).
After repair: loss of control of wind or stool, urgency, soiling (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.3).
Urinary retention, incontinence or urgency (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.3).
Painful intercourse and pain at the scar (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.3).
physicalSigns: Bleeding from the perineum after the third stage (clinical judgment).
Torn perineum extending to the anal margin or muscle ends visible (Oman MOH guideline, Section 4.0).
Loss of the normal anal ring or gaping anus on rectal examination (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5.1).
Wound redness, swelling, discharge or breakdown after repair (clinical judgment).
redFlags: Torn skin reaching the anal margin: treat as a third degree tear and call a senior obstetrician before any suturing (Oman MOH guideline, Section 4.0).
Heavy bleeding with signs of shock after birth: resuscitate and call for help (clinical judgment).
Rectal mucosa torn or faecal contamination: fourth degree or buttonhole tear needing theatre repair and antibiotics (Oman MOH guideline, Section 2.1).
Passage of stool or wind through the vagina after repair: suspect a rectovaginal fistula and refer (Oman MOH guideline, Section 2.1).
Fever, severe perineal pain, offensive discharge or wound breakdown: assess for infection and dehiscence (clinical judgment).
precipitants: First vaginal birth: obstetric anal sphincter injury in 6.1% of first births against 1.7% of later births (Oman MOH guideline, Section 01).
Forceps delivery, baby over 4 kg, persistent occipito-posterior position, shoulder dystocia, prolonged second stage (Oman MOH guideline, Section 3.1).
Midline episiotomy; mediolateral episiotomy angled away from the midline is advised if needed (Oman MOH guideline, Section 3.0).
Induction of labour and epidural analgesia (Oman MOH guideline, Section 3.1).
Previous sphincter injury: recurrence is estimated at 4 to 8% (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.3).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Rectal lining torn but the anal sphincter is intact; must be documented separately and repaired (Oman MOH guideline, Section 2.1).
Both sphincters and the anal lining are torn (Oman MOH guideline, Section 02).
Perineal muscle torn, sphincter intact on rectal examination (Oman MOH guideline, Section 02).
Persistent bleeding with a firm contracted uterus; needs speculum examination (clinical judgment).
Severe pain and a tense, bruised swelling after repair (clinical judgment).

clinicalManagement.title: Examine systematically before suturing
actions: Explain and obtain consent; examine in good light with the woman comfortable and analgesia in place (Oman MOH guideline, Section 4.0).
Perform a vaginal and rectal examination to find the full extent of the injury, and grade the tear (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5.1).
Treat any skin tear reaching the anal margin as third degree until proven otherwise; if in doubt about the grade, choose the higher (Oman MOH guideline, Section 02 and Section 4.0).
Call a senior obstetrician for a suspected third or fourth degree tear or rectal buttonhole tear (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.1.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Repair first and second degree tears
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible after birth
actions: Give local anaesthetic by infiltration, aspirating before each injection, within the label maximum (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration).
First degree tears that are not bleeding or distorting anatomy may heal without sutures; otherwise repair the vaginal wall, perineal muscle and skin in layers (clinical judgment).
Check the repair with a rectal examination to exclude stitches through the anal lining (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.1.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Repair third and fourth degree tears in theatre
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible, in an operating theatre
actions: Transfer to theatre for 3b, 3c, fourth degree or buttonhole tears; consider theatre for 3a if lighting, analgesia or asepsis in the birth room is inadequate (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.1.1).
Use regional or general anaesthesia so that sphincter muscle relaxes and the ends can be brought together without tension (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5.1).
Give the pre-repair antibiotics (see medicines) (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1).
Repair the anal lining with 3-0 polyglactin or 2-0 polyglactin, knots tied in the lumen, or a continuous submucosal stitch (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5.1).
Repair the internal sphincter separately with interrupted or mattress fine sutures such as 3-0 polydioxanone, without overlap (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5).
Repair the external sphincter by overlap or end-to-end approximation; use end-to-end for partial thickness tears (3a and some 3b) (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5).

Rebuild the perineal body, bury the knots under the superficial perineal muscles, and do a final rectal examination (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5.1; NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.1.1).
Obtain consent that covers flatus or faecal incontinence and fistula (Oman MOH guideline, Section 5.1).

clinicalManagement.title: Postnatal care and medicines
actions: Leave a bladder catheter in for at least 24 hours (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1).
Give oral antibiotics, a stool softener and regular analgesia (see medicines) (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1; NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1).

Advise perineal hygiene with water, support of the perineum when opening bowels, coughing and sneezing, and avoiding straining (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.2; NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.1.2).
Offer ice packs for short periods in the first 72 hours, with caution because they can reduce blood supply (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.1.2 and Section 3.3).
Check for urinary and bowel problems before discharge (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Follow up and plan the next birth
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 6 to 12 weeks and in the next pregnancy
actions: Refer to physiotherapy for pelvic floor exercises and book a urogynaecology review 6 to 12 weeks after repair (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.2).
Explain the extent of the tear and that 60 to 80% are symptom free at 12 months (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.3).
If incontinence or pain persists, refer to a urogynaecologist or colorectal surgeon and consider endoanal ultrasound and manometry (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.3).

In the next pregnancy discuss the mode of birth early and again at about 36 weeks; offer caesarean section if the woman has symptoms or abnormal ultrasound or manometry (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.4; NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Section 3.3).
Document the structures torn, the repair method, suture materials, counselling and file an incident report (Oman MOH guideline, Documentation).

regimens.indication: Local anaesthesia for repair of a perineal tear
regimens.patientGroup: Woman with a first or second degree tear or the perineal layer of a sphincter repair
regimens.dose: Infiltrate the lowest volume of 1% lidocaine that gives anaesthesia; do not exceed the label maximum dose (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration). Dilution and preparation: none; use the 1% solution as supplied; preservative-free single-dose vials are used for infiltration.
regimens.route: Local infiltration into the perineal tissues; aspirate before each injection to avoid intravascular injection (Xylocaine label, Warnings and Precautions)
regimens.frequency: Once before repair; top up within the maximum dose if needed
adjustments: Use with caution in severe liver disease because amide anaesthetics are metabolised in the liver (Xylocaine label, Precautions).
Resuscitation equipment and oxygen must be available (Xylocaine label, Warnings).
Methaemoglobinaemia risk with other oxidising drugs (Xylocaine label, Precautions).

Use epinephrine-free solution for large volumes only as the label allows; the label states solutions with epinephrine are used when larger volumes are needed (Xylocaine label, Dosage and Administration).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Signs of toxicity: perioral numbness, dizziness, tinnitus, convulsions (Xylocaine label, Adverse Reactions).
Blood pressure, pulse and consciousness after injection (Xylocaine label, Warnings).
contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to amide-type local anaesthetics (Xylocaine label, Contraindications).

regimens.sourceEdition: Xylocaine MPF label, Section Indications and Usage, Section Contraindications and Section Dosage and Administration

regimens.indication: Prophylaxis for repair of a third or fourth degree tear
regimens.patientGroup: Women with obstetric anal sphincter injury or rectal buttonhole tear
regimens.dose: 2 g (3 g if the woman weighs more than 120 kg) as a single dose before the repair (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1). Dilution and preparation: reconstitute each 1 g vial with 2.5 mL of sterile water for injection (about 330 mg/mL), shake well; for direct injection dilute further with about 5 mL of sterile water and inject slowly over 3 to 5 minutes; for infusion dilute in 50 to 100 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose (Cefazolin label, Reconstitution and Administration).
regimens.route: Intravenous injection over 3 to 5 minutes, or intravenous infusion; the label allows intramuscular use into a large muscle mass
regimens.frequency: Single dose, 30 to 60 minutes before the start of repair
regimens.duration: Single dose (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1)
adjustments: The label dose for pre-operative prophylaxis is 1 g; the NSW rule dose of 2 g is higher than the label (Cefazolin label, Perioperative Prophylactic Use).
Renal impairment: reduce the interval or dose per the label for repeated dosing (Cefazolin label, Dosage).
Penicillin allergy that is only mild or delayed may allow a cephalosporin; severe immediate reaction needs the alternative below (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Watch for hypersensitivity during and after injection (Cefazolin label, Warnings).
Diarrhoea after antibiotics may be Clostridioides difficile colitis (Cefazolin label, Warnings).
contraindications: Known allergy to the cephalosporin group of antibiotics (Cefazolin label, Contraindications).
regimens.branch: Antibiotics for obstetric anal sphincter injury
regimens.useWhen: Preferred when there is no severe penicillin or cephalosporin hypersensitivity.

regimens.indication: Prophylaxis for repair of a third or fourth degree tear in severe penicillin allergy
regimens.patientGroup: Women with obstetric anal sphincter injury and severe penicillin hypersensitivity
regimens.dose: 600 mg as a single dose before the repair (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1). Dilution and preparation: dilute 600 mg in 50 mL of compatible fluid (0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose); the final concentration must not exceed 18 mg/mL and the rate must not exceed 30 mg per minute; infuse over 20 minutes; never inject undiluted as a bolus (Clindamycin label, Dosage and Administration).
regimens.duration: Single dose (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1)
adjustments: Contains benzyl alcohol as preservative (Clindamycin label, Description).
No dose change in renal disease; caution in moderate to severe liver disease (Clindamycin label, Precautions).
Do not follow with oral co-amoxiclav in a woman with severe penicillin hypersensitivity; use the local alternative course (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1).
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register returned an empty page from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.
monitoring: Diarrhoea during or after treatment: Clostridioides difficile colitis (Clindamycin label, Warnings).
Skin rash and hypersensitivity (Clindamycin label, Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: History of hypersensitivity to clindamycin or lincomycin (Clindamycin label, Contraindications).
regimens.branch: Antibiotics for obstetric anal sphincter injury
regimens.useWhen: Choose when there is a history of immediate severe or delayed severe hypersensitivity to penicillin.

regimens.indication: Anaerobic cover for repair of a third or fourth degree tear
regimens.patientGroup: Women with obstetric anal sphincter injury or rectal buttonhole tear
regimens.dose: 500 mg as a single dose with the pre-repair antibiotic (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1). Dilution and preparation: use the ready-made 500 mg per 100 mL isotonic solution; no dilution; do not use with aluminium needles.
regimens.route: Intravenous infusion over about one hour (Metronidazole label, Dosage and Administration)
regimens.duration: Single dose (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1)
adjustments: Take no alcohol during treatment because of a disulfiram-like reaction (Metronidazole label, Contraindications).
Severe liver disease: reduce the dose (Metronidazole label, Precautions).

monitoring: Nausea, metallic taste and neurological symptoms with longer courses (Metronidazole label, Adverse Reactions).
Thrombophlebitis at the infusion site (Metronidazole label, Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to metronidazole or other nitroimidazoles (Metronidazole label, Contraindications).
Disulfiram taken within the last 2 weeks (Metronidazole label, Contraindications).

regimens.indication: Antibiotic course after repair of a third or fourth degree tear
regimens.patientGroup: Women after sphincter repair without severe penicillin hypersensitivity
regimens.dose: 875 mg/125 mg one tablet every 12 hours for five days (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1); the Oman guideline asks for oral antibiotics to complete 7 days of treatment (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1). Dilution and preparation: none; oral tablet.
regimens.route: Oral, swallowed whole at the start of a meal to improve absorption of clavulanate and reduce stomach upset (Co-amoxiclav label, Dosage and Administration)
regimens.duration: 5 days (NSW rule) or 7 days (Oman guideline); choose per the unit protocol
adjustments: Do not use the 875 mg/125 mg tablet if glomerular filtration rate is below 30 mL/min (Co-amoxiclav label, Dosage).
Breastfeeding: amoxicillin passes into milk; watch the infant for diarrhoea or thrush (Co-amoxiclav label, Nursing mothers).
Mild or delayed non-severe penicillin allergy: the NSW rule uses cephalexin plus metronidazole (NSW Royal Hospital for Women rule, Table 1).

monitoring: Diarrhoea and signs of Clostridioides difficile colitis (Co-amoxiclav label, Warnings).
Liver function if prolonged or repeated (Co-amoxiclav label, Warnings).
Rash or allergy (Co-amoxiclav label, Adverse Reactions).
contraindications: History of serious hypersensitivity reaction to amoxicillin, clavulanate or other beta-lactam antibiotics (Co-amoxiclav label, Contraindications).
Previous cholestatic jaundice or liver dysfunction with amoxicillin and clavulanate (Co-amoxiclav label, Contraindications).

regimens.indication: Stool softening to avoid straining after sphincter repair (off-label)
regimens.patientGroup: Women after repair of a third or fourth degree tear
regimens.dose: 15 mL (10 g) twice daily for 10 days to 2 weeks (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1). Dilution and preparation: none; oral solution, may be mixed with water or juice; adjust the dose to give soft stools.
regimens.route: Oral, measured with a spoon or cup (Lactulose label, Description)
regimens.duration: 10 days to 2 weeks (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1)

Reduce the dose or stop if diarrhoea occurs (Lactulose label, Adverse Reactions).

monitoring: Stool consistency and absence of straining (Oman MOH guideline, Section 6.1).

contraindications: Patients who require a low-galactose diet (Lactulose label, Contraindications).

guidelineComparison.note: The Jeddah series found grade III in 79.5% and grade IV in 8.0% of 112 women with sphincter injury, an incidence of 0.93% of vaginal births.

teaching.scope: Woman with a perineal tear after vaginal birth: systematic perineal and rectal examination, grading from first to fourth degree, repair of first and second degree tears with local anaesthetic, theatre repair of third and fourth degree tears (obstetric anal sphincter injury, OASIS), antibiotics, laxatives and analgesia, follow-up and advice for a future birth. Uses the Oman Ministry of Health Royal Hospital guideline (based on RCOG Green-top 29) and the Royal Hospital for Women (NSW) business rule; a Saudi single-centre study supplies local incidence. No Saudi national guideline was found.
learningObjectives: Examine every perineum before suturing and grade the tear.
Repair third and fourth degree tears in theatre with good anaesthesia and light.
Give antibiotics, a stool softener and pain relief after sphincter repair.
Arrange physiotherapy and a review at 6 to 12 weeks, and plan the next birth.
pitfalls: Using bulking agents together with laxatives.
Leaving the sphincter repair to an untrained clinician or doing it without good anaesthesia.
Not documenting the structures torn and the sutures used.
keyPoints: Skin tears reaching the anal margin are third degree until proven otherwise.
Repair the internal sphincter separately and the external sphincter by overlap or end-to-end.
Catheter for at least 24 hours and stool softener for 10 days to 2 weeks.
Offer caesarean section in the next birth if symptoms or abnormal ultrasound.

patientEducation: You had a tear during birth; keep the area clean and dry with water only.
Take your pain relief, antibiotics and laxative as prescribed.
Support the stitches with a pad when you open your bowels, cough or sneeze, and do not strain.
Tell us if you have fever, a bad smell, severe pain, loss of control of wind or stool, or trouble passing urine.
Do pelvic floor exercises and come to your review 6 to 12 weeks after birth.
Discuss how you want to give birth next time early in your next pregnancy.
lifestyleAndDiet: Drink plenty of fluids and eat fibre-rich food.
Rest and avoid heavy lifting at first.
Breastfeed lying on your side if sitting is painful.
Do not use tampons or have intercourse until healed and reviewed.
Take a rolled towel or cushion to relieve pressure when sitting.
mdtReferrals: Obstetrician and gynaecologist; midwife; anaesthetist; colorectal surgeon; urogynaecologist; physiotherapist; pharmacist; infection control team.
dischargeCriteria: Tear grade and structures involved documented; repair method and suture materials recorded; catheter removed and voiding checked; antibiotics, laxative and analgesia prescribed with clear instructions; physiotherapy referral and 6 to 12 week review booked; warning signs and contact number given.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Medical review within 48 hours; physiotherapy referral at discharge; urogynaecology review 6 to 12 weeks after sphincter repair; endoanal ultrasound and manometry if symptoms persist; discuss mode of birth at the start of the next pregnancy and at about 36 weeks.
